title: The Descent
author: Alexandre Dias
contentWarnings: Themes of obsession and voluntary disappearance
excerpt: The marker was set at four hundred and eighteen meters. Frantisek had placed it there in 1997. Studna was, everyone had agreed for decades, a four-hundred-and-eighteen-meter cave. Marek Hájek had believed this for thirty years. He was, on a June expedition in the twenty-ninth year, seven hundred meters underground and about to find out otherwise.

chapters.title: The Marker
chapters.body:
The marker was set at four hundred and eighteen meters.

It had been placed there by Frantisek Mikolaj in the summer of 1997, and it had stood, undisturbed, for twenty-nine years. It was a small aluminum peg driven into a crack in the limestone, with a red plastic tag threaded through the eyelet at the top on which had been written, in the specific serif hand of a Czech caver who had learned his letters under the last decades of the Warsaw Pact:

*Konec. Frantisek 4.VII.97.*

*End. Frantisek 4 July 97.*

Marek Hájek had known Frantisek. He had, in fact, first entered a cave under Frantisek's supervision, at the age of nineteen, at the small training crag south of Brno where the caving club had run its beginner sessions for four decades. He had been shown, that first summer, how to abseil, and how to prusik back up a fixed rope, and how to keep a small orange notebook in a waterproof case at his hip on which to write, in pencil that would not smudge, whatever he found. He had, in the years since, spent a considerable portion of his adult life in caves, and had, at forty-eight, made his own small name in the specific narrow world of Slovakian and Moravian caving, and had taken over, upon Frantisek's death eleven years earlier, the small club at which he had first been trained.

He was, in June of the twenty-ninth year, seven hundred meters underground.

He had been in the Studna cave system for three days. Studna was, at nine hundred and twelve meters of surveyed depth, the second deepest known cave in the country, and had been Frantisek's project for the last twelve years of his caving life. Frantisek had, in 1997, pushed the deepest point known then — four hundred and eighteen meters, at the bottom of the pitch known as the Konec Shaft — and had, at that depth, set the aluminum peg. He had returned in subsequent years to see whether he could push further, and had, each time, come back to say that the cave did not go on: that below the peg was a small chamber, and below the chamber was a low silty passage that pinched off after twelve meters, and that Studna terminated there.

Two subsequent expeditions in the early two-thousands, run by younger cavers, had reached the same conclusion. The silty passage did not go. Studna was a four-hundred-and-eighteen-meter cave.

Then, in 2011, a young caver named Ondrej Vejr had, on a solo push that had been formally frowned upon and quietly celebrated, discovered a small hole in the ceiling of the silty passage, roughly halfway along its length, and had squeezed through it into a new pitch. That pitch had been surveyed the following year to a depth of six hundred and twelve meters, and had, over the next decade, been extended, pitch by pitch, by successive expeditions of the club, down to the current surveyed maximum of nine hundred and twelve.

The current bottom of Studna was, in June of the twenty-ninth year, a small sump — a passage filled to the roof with cold clear water — at nine hundred and twelve meters below the surface entrance, and had been for the last three years the deepest known point in the country not accessible only to specialist cave divers.

Marek had, on this expedition, come down to the sump.

He had come with two others — Katka, thirty-two, who had done every deep expedition of the last five years, and Jozef, forty-one, who had been his partner on the surveys of the seven hundred and eight hundred meter horizons — and they had, over the first two days, established the camp at six hundred meters that the club maintained as a base for deep pushes. On the third day they had descended the last three hundred meters to the sump, and had surveyed a small side passage that had been noted on previous trips but never entered, and had found it to pinch off after eight meters, and had returned to the sump for lunch.

They had eaten their sandwiches on a small dry ledge above the water.

Marek had looked at the sump.

The sump was, as sumps went, unremarkable. It was cold. The water was clear. The visible portion of the passage disappeared under the roof at a depth of perhaps a meter and a half. Cave divers had, in 2019, made a preliminary exploration of the sump and had reported that it continued as an underwater passage for at least twenty meters before their air had turned them back. It was, on the club's map, the terminus of Studna.

Marek had said, over his sandwich: *has anyone been up there?*

Katka had said: *up where.*

He had pointed. Above the sump, in the ceiling of the small chamber that contained it, was a section of limestone about three meters up that had a small dark alcove in it. It was not, at first glance, particularly promising. It was the sort of ceiling feature that one might, in a cave one was casually exploring, notice and pass over, because ceiling alcoves rarely led anywhere.

Katka had said: *no. Never noticed it, actually.*

Jozef had said: *nothing on the survey up there.*

Marek had said: *let me see.*

He had stood up. He had, with the small careful movements of a caver who had been at seven hundred meters underground for two days and knew his own tiredness, worked his way up the wall of the chamber using the natural handholds in the limestone, and had, at the alcove, reached his head in and shone his light.

The alcove had gone back.

It had gone back further than he had expected. His light, at first, had shown only a small horizontal tube about half a meter across, running back into the rock. He had extended the light. He had followed the tube with his eyes. It had continued, at that diameter, for perhaps eight meters, and had then opened.

It had opened into another chamber.

He had lowered himself back down to Katka and Jozef.

He had said, without particular emphasis: *there is something up there.*

—

The three of them had climbed the wall.

They had, one at a time, worked their way up into the alcove and along the tube. The tube had been tight — Marek had, at one point, had to exhale to squeeze through a section that had narrowed to about forty centimeters — but it had, as he had seen, opened after eight meters into a chamber, and the chamber, when the three of them had assembled inside it and had shone their combined lights around, had turned out to be substantial.

It had been perhaps twenty meters across. The ceiling had been perhaps ten meters above them. The floor had been a broken mess of large limestone blocks that had, at some point in the recent geological past, fallen from the ceiling and lodged themselves in a rough talus. On the far side of the chamber, opposite the entrance tube, had been a further passage — a wide, roughly triangular opening about four meters high at its apex, leading further into the mountain.

Marek had stood in the middle of the chamber.

He had said: *this is not on the map.*

Katka had said: *no.*

Jozef had said: *we should go back.*

Marek had said: *what?*

Jozef had said: *we should go back to the camp. We should report this. We should organize a proper expedition. This is not what we came down here for.*

Marek had said: *we can look. We are here. Just a look.*

Jozef had said: *Marek.*

Marek had looked at Jozef.

He had understood, in that look, that Jozef was going to insist. That Jozef, at forty-one, with a wife and two children in Bratislava, was the responsible partner on the trip, and was going to say now what needed to be said — that they were three people at nine hundred meters underground with camp two days away and enough supplies for one more day of pushing at the sump, and that they were not, by any of the club's rules, in a position to begin an unmapped exploration of a new chamber deep in a cave system.

Marek had also understood, in that same moment, that he was going to go into the passage.

He had understood this without deliberation. He had, in the moment of shining his light through the entrance tube, decided. He had spent thirty years of his life caving in this country. He had spent twenty-nine of those years knowing the aluminum peg at four hundred and eighteen meters, and had, in the last fifteen years, watched Ondrej Vejr's small hole in the ceiling become the doorway to a further five hundred meters of Studna, and had known, ever since, that the cave was still going. And now he was standing at nine hundred meters, in a chamber that was not on the map, looking at a passage that led further.

He was going in.

He had said: *Jozef. Ten minutes. Just ten meters into the passage. I want to see the character of it.*

Jozef had said: *ten minutes.*

Marek had said: *ten meters. Just to see. I promise.*

Jozef had held his gaze.

Katka, who had, throughout the exchange, been standing at Marek's shoulder, had said quietly: *I will go with him.*

Jozef had said: *no.*

Katka had said: *Jozef.*

Jozef had said, more quietly: *one of us has to stay at the tube. If something happens.*

Katka had, after a moment, nodded. She had said: *I will stay.*

Marek had said: *ten meters. Ten minutes.*

He had gone into the passage.

—

He had not, in the event, kept to ten meters.

He had walked forward into the passage, and had, at the ten-meter mark, seen that the passage continued to descend, at a mild gradient, into a further widening. He had walked another ten meters. He had, at twenty, seen that the passage widened further, and that it curved gently to the left, and that it opened, at what he estimated to be twenty-five meters, into another chamber.

He had gone to the chamber.

The chamber had been bigger than the first. It had been, so far as his headlamp had been able to determine in the dark, perhaps thirty meters across. Its ceiling had been not visible. Its floor had continued to slope downward, at the same mild gradient.

He had, standing in the second chamber, understood two things.

He had understood, first, that he had been down for perhaps five minutes and had already exceeded his promised ten meters by a factor of two, and would, if he wanted to keep to the ten-minute limit, have to turn back within about a minute.

He had understood, second, that the second chamber was not the last. It was, from where he was standing, obvious that the passage continued from the far wall — he could see the darker patch that indicated an opening, at the level of his feet, on the far side of the chamber — and it was obvious that the passage was descending.

He had, in his small quick mental arithmetic, estimated the vertical distance he had already lost from the level of the sump: perhaps twelve meters. Which meant that he was, at the moment he stood in the second chamber, at nine hundred and twenty-four meters below the surface.

He was, in other words, already at the deepest point that had ever been recorded in the country.

He had turned. He had walked back down the passage. He had emerged, on schedule, into the first chamber. Katka had been at the tube, waiting. Jozef had been in the tube itself, halfway in, watching him come back with the specific weary patience of a man who had known the ten minutes were going to be more than ten minutes.

Marek had said: *we need to come back.*

Jozef had said: *of course we need to come back.*

Marek had said: *with a full expedition. Proper survey team. Camp at nine hundred.*

Jozef had said: *yes.*

Marek had said: *I want to lead it.*

Jozef had looked at him.

Jozef had said: *of course you want to lead it.*

They had begun, together, the long climb back up.

chapters.title: The Camp at Nine Hundred
chapters.body:
The proper expedition took nine months to organize.

Marek spent the winter and spring writing proposals — to the club, to the national caving federation, to the small foundation that funded serious expedition work in the region — and organizing supplies and personnel. He recruited a team of six. He himself, as expedition leader. Katka, as second in command. Jozef had, after several long conversations in a small pub in Bratislava that Marek did not enjoy remembering, declined to participate — he had said, quietly, over his second beer, that he did not think the new passage should be pushed at all, and that if it was going to be pushed he would prefer not to be part of it. Marek had understood. He had, since that afternoon at the sump, understood a great many things about Jozef that he had not previously understood, and had understood also that he was, himself, on the other side of a small line that Jozef had refused to cross.

He had replaced Jozef with a younger caver named Pavel, a twenty-six-year-old who had done two of the deep pushes the previous year and who wanted, obviously, to be involved in whatever came next. He had recruited three others — a surveyor from Prague, a rigging specialist from Poland, and a medic who had done cave work in the Balkans — and had, by early spring, assembled his team of six.

They had gone down in mid-April.

They had established the camp at six hundred over the first two days, and had then, over the following four, established a second camp at nine hundred meters, in the first of the new chambers. It was called, on the survey map they had begun to draw, Marek's Chamber. Marek had, when Katka had suggested this, said no. She had said it anyway, on the map. He had not, in the end, insisted.

They had begun the survey of the passage.

The passage had gone on for a long time.

The first chamber — Marek's Chamber — was at nine hundred and twelve meters. The second chamber, which they now called Konec II, in a small joke about Frantisek's peg, was at nine hundred and twenty-four. The passage from Konec II continued to descend, at the same mild gradient, and opened, after another twenty-two meters, into a third chamber at nine hundred and thirty-seven. From the third chamber the passage continued.

At nine hundred and fifty they entered a fourth chamber. At nine hundred and seventy-two they entered a fifth. At nine hundred and ninety-four they entered a sixth.

The team had, by the fourth day of the survey, become quiet.

Marek had noticed the quiet. He had, on the fifth day, at the six-hundred-camp above during the rest cycle, tried to name it. He had said, over his cup of instant coffee, in the small chamber the six of them had rigged with hammocks: *is it just me, or is everyone thinking about it?*

Pavel had said: *thinking about what.*

Marek had said: *how far it goes.*

Katka had said: *it should stop.*

The surveyor from Prague, whose name was Milan, had said: *it will stop.*

Marek had said: *when.*

Milan had looked at him.

Milan had said: *it always stops. Caves stop. That is what caves do.*

Marek had said: *this one has not stopped.*

Milan had said: *it has not stopped yet.*

They had drunk their coffee.

The rigger, Wojciech, had said, quietly: *my grandfather was in caves. In the Tatras. He told me a story once, when I was a boy. There was, he said, a cave in the eastern Tatras that was known, before the war, to go on for very far. Kilometers, he said. He did not say how many. And the people in the villages around it had a name for it. They called it the mouth. And they said that the cave did not have a bottom, that it went down forever, and that any caver who went into it and did not come back had been swallowed.*

Wojciech had paused.

He had said: *I have never believed the story. I have thought it was, you know, a story. Something old men told to boys.*

Pavel had said: *and now?*

Wojciech had said: *now I am not sure.*

They had sat in the small chamber at six hundred meters below the surface of Slovakia, in April, in the middle of an expedition that had gone farther than any of them had planned, and they had not, for perhaps five minutes, spoken.

Then Marek had said: *we go on tomorrow.*

Katka had said: *Marek.*

Marek had said: *I want to reach a thousand.*

Katka had said: *and then?*

Marek had said: *and then we see.*

They had agreed. They had, later that evening, agreed to descend the next morning to Marek's Chamber, and to push the passage from the sixth chamber onward, and to see where they got by evening.

Marek, lying in his hammock at six hundred meters that night, in the specific total darkness of a cave in which every light had been switched off for the sleep cycle, had understood something.

He had understood that he had been waiting, for the whole of the last thirty years, for a cave to keep going.

He had spent his adult life going down small caves that had all, in the end, stopped. He had spent his adult life reaching the last chamber, the last silt-choked passage, the last sump, and had turned back and gone home each time. He had, in some quiet interior place he had not consulted, hoped that one of them would not stop. He had hoped that he would, at some point, walk into a chamber, and shine his light forward, and see a passage that continued, and continue into it, and find another passage, and continue, and keep on continuing until he was, at some depth beyond any depth previously recorded, in a cave that did not have a bottom.

He had, at four hundred and eighteen meters twenty-nine years ago, learned the shape of this hope from Frantisek. Frantisek had told him, at the peg, that this was where Studna ended, and had turned back with him and Katka's father — who had come as their guide, Katka not yet born — and had gone up. Marek had, at nineteen, felt an obscure disappointment. He had wanted, though he had not known he wanted, for Frantisek to say *no. It goes on. Follow me.* And they would have gone on together.

He was, thirty years later, at nine hundred and twelve meters, having lived long enough to walk with his own team into a chamber where the cave, at last, had not stopped.

He was going to walk into the next chamber, and the next, and the next, and see how far he could go.

—

By the ninth day they had reached one thousand and fifty-two meters.

They had surveyed twelve chambers past Marek's Chamber. Each chamber had been a little larger than the last. The passages between them had continued to descend at the same mild gradient. There had been, along the way, three small side passages that they had briefly investigated and found to pinch off after a few meters — these had been reassuring, in a way, because they had suggested that the main passage was, at least, part of an ordinary cave system, with the ordinary distribution of dead-end branches. But the main passage itself had not stopped.

At one thousand and fifty-two meters — Milan had called this depth to Marek, over the survey radio, from where he was sitting in the twelfth chamber with his laser rangefinder — they had, all of them, understood that they were in the deepest known cave in Central Europe.

They had reached this depth on the ninth morning.

By the ninth evening, having pushed another two hundred and twelve meters and surveyed six more chambers, they were at one thousand two hundred and sixty-four.

Marek had, that night, back at the camp at nine hundred, made a decision.

He had said, over their small meal of freeze-dried curry: *we are running out of supplies. We should reprovision from the surface. But I do not want to lose the momentum. So I propose that half of us go up tomorrow, resupply, and come back down in three days. And the other half stay at the camp and rest.*

Katka had said: *and continue pushing.*

Marek had said: *no. Rest.*

Katka had held his gaze for a moment. She had, he thought, been about to challenge him. But she had, in the end, only nodded.

They had drawn lots. Katka, Pavel, and Wojciech had drawn the surface trip. Marek, Milan, and the medic — a tall quiet woman named Ana — had drawn to stay.

The surface team had left the following morning.

—

They had not, the surface team, returned in three days.

Marek and Milan and Ana had rested for the first day. They had slept a great deal. They had, on the second day, done some small housekeeping around the camp — checked the ropes on the main pitches, resurveyed a small section of Marek's Chamber that Milan had wanted to redo — and had, on the third day, in the absence of the returning team, become quiet.

They had waited.

On the fourth day, Marek had said, aloud, at the camp: *I want to go down.*

Ana had said: *without the survey team.*

Marek had said: *just to look. Just a short push. To see whether the passage keeps going past Chamber Eighteen.*

Milan had said: *Marek, no.*

Marek had said: *just me. Just a short push. Two hours. You stay here.*

Milan had said: *the protocol is that no one caves alone in this system. You wrote the protocol.*

Marek had said: *I know I wrote the protocol.*

They had looked at each other, in the specific way of two men who have known each other's decisions for many years.

Milan had said: *I will come with you.*

Ana had said: *and I will wait at the camp.*

They had gone down together on the morning of the fourth day.

They had passed through the twelve chambers they had already surveyed. They had reached Chamber Eighteen. They had continued into the passage beyond.

The passage had continued to descend.

They had, by lunchtime, entered Chamber Nineteen. It had been at one thousand two hundred and eighty-eight meters. It had been, so far as they could tell in the light of their two headlamps, unusually large — perhaps forty meters across, with a ceiling too high to see. The floor had continued to slope downward.

They had eaten their small lunch on a boulder in the middle of Chamber Nineteen.

Milan had said, over his sandwich: *Marek.*

Marek had said: *yes.*

Milan had said: *what are we going to do if this goes to two thousand meters.*

Marek had chewed his sandwich.

He had said: *we survey it.*

Milan had said: *and if it goes to three thousand.*

Marek had said: *we survey it.*

Milan had said: *there is a limit.*

Marek had said: *is there?*

Milan had looked at him.

Milan had said: *at some point the rock gives out. At some point the water table is above us. At some point the passage floods, or squeezes off, or ends.*

Marek had said: *yes.*

Milan had said: *but you do not think it will.*

Marek had put down his sandwich.

He had looked at Milan.

He had said, quietly: *I do not think it will.*

Milan had, after a moment, put down his own sandwich.

He had said: *why not.*

Marek had said: *I do not know why not. I know only that since the first day I stood in the entrance to Marek's Chamber, I have known this passage goes on. I have known it in the same way I know how tall I am, or how many fingers I have. It is a fact I have not been able to argue with. I have kept it to myself because it is not a fact that permits itself to be said in a survey report.*

*But I am saying it now.*

*The passage does not end.*

Milan had, for a long moment, looked at him.

Milan had said: *I want to go back up.*

Marek had said: *I know.*

Milan had said: *now, Marek. I want to go back to the camp now. And I want us to go up to the surface tomorrow, whether or not the resupply team has come back. And I want us to close this cave.*

Marek had said: *you know I cannot do that.*

Milan had said: *I know.*

Milan had stood up. He had, quite calmly, put on his pack. He had said: *I am going back to the camp. Ana and I will wait for you until tonight. If you are not back by tonight we will go up.*

Marek had said: *Milan.*

Milan had said: *do what you are going to do.*

Milan had walked out of Chamber Nineteen.

Marek had watched him go.

He had sat on the boulder for perhaps another ten minutes, finishing his sandwich, drinking the last of the tea in his flask.

Then he had put on his own pack, and he had continued into the passage.

chapters.title: Below
chapters.body:
He walked for a very long time.

He did not, at any point, feel that he was walking downhill in the sense that his knees felt the strain of descent — the gradient was too mild for that — but he understood, from the small careful mental accounting he had been performing since he had left Milan in Chamber Nineteen, that he was, on average, losing between three and four vertical meters per horizontal hundred. He was, at that rate, dropping about twenty meters an hour.

He walked through Chamber Twenty at one thousand two hundred and ninety-five meters.

He walked through Chamber Twenty-one at one thousand three hundred and eleven.

He walked through Chamber Twenty-two at one thousand three hundred and twenty-nine.

The chambers had grown similar to each other. Each was between twenty and forty meters across, with a ceiling high enough not to be easily visible, a floor of broken limestone blocks, and a further passage exiting from the opposite side of the entry passage. He had ceased, by Chamber Twenty-three, to pause and note the character of each chamber. He was, he understood, no longer doing science.

He was walking.

He was walking in the way a man might walk across a field in the summer if the field went on for a very long time. He was walking without thinking about the walking. He was walking in the same quiet steady rhythm one walked when one had been walking for hours and had ceased to notice the walking as an activity. He was walking, in some sense, because the walking was itself the point.

At Chamber Twenty-five he sat down.

He sat down on a small block, and he took out his water bottle, and he drank. He checked his watch. He had been walking for four hours since leaving Milan. Milan had, by his instructions, been going to wait at the nine-hundred camp until nightfall, and had by now surely gone up to look for the resupply team, and would probably by now be at six hundred meters, and would probably by tomorrow morning be at the surface.

He was, in other words, alone in the cave. Ana would have gone up with Milan. There was no one below him. There was no one likely to be below him for at least a day.

He sat and looked at his watch.

He thought, for the first time since leaving Chamber Nineteen, about what he was doing.

He was, he understood, doing exactly what Jozef had feared he would do that afternoon at the sump. He was pushing an unmapped passage without support, without a partner, without a survey, without any of the safeguards he himself had spent thirty years insisting on in every other context. He was, in the caving sense, behaving irresponsibly. He was, in the wider sense, doing something that, if it went badly, would end with a rescue operation that would kill several people trying to recover his body from thirteen hundred meters below the surface.

He knew all of this.

He was going on.

He was going on because the passage was still descending, and because at some point today, or tomorrow, or perhaps the day after, he was going to reach the bottom of it, or he was going to prove — in the small quiet way of a man in a cave at thirteen hundred meters — that it did not have one.

He put his water bottle away. He stood up. He continued.

—

At one thousand four hundred meters he began to be aware of a sound.

He had been walking for perhaps five hours when he noticed it. It was faint. It was, at first, at the very edge of what he could distinguish from the ordinary silence of the cave — the small hiss of his own breath, the small clicks of his boots on the rock, the distant sound of falling water that he had been hearing for the last three chambers.

The sound was none of these.

He stopped walking. He turned off his headlamp.

He stood in the absolute darkness of the cave, and he listened.

The sound was steady. It was low. It was, so far as he could tell, coming from the direction he had been walking — from further down the passage, further into the cave, at some distance he could not estimate. It was not water. It was not wind. It was not the ordinary settling of rock. It was, more than anything, a *breathing* — the specific slow deep rhythmic sound of some very large body drawing in air and letting it out, at a rate of perhaps one breath every eight to ten seconds.

He listened.

He listened for perhaps a full minute.

He turned his headlamp back on.

He continued walking.

—

He walked for another three hours before he saw it.

He walked through Chamber Twenty-six at one thousand four hundred and twenty. He walked through Chamber Twenty-seven at one thousand four hundred and thirty-eight. He walked through Chamber Twenty-eight at one thousand four hundred and fifty-nine.

At Chamber Twenty-nine the passage widened suddenly.

He had, until then, been walking through chambers of a similar size, connected by passages of a similar diameter. At Chamber Twenty-nine the passage opened, without warning, into a space so large that his headlamp, playing across it, could not find the far wall. The floor continued to slope downward in front of him. The ceiling was invisible. The room, so far as his light could determine, was enormous.

He stood at the mouth of the chamber.

The breathing was, at that distance, no longer faint. It was clearly audible. It was, if anything, coming from the space in front of him — from somewhere in the enormous room, at some depth further into it. It was the same slow deep rhythm he had been hearing for hours. He could feel it, now, faintly, in his chest — the small pressure change of a very large exhalation, at intervals of eight to ten seconds, reaching him across the chamber.

He walked into the room.

He walked for perhaps ten minutes. The floor continued to slope downward. He passed, along the way, several large blocks of limestone that had fallen at some point from the invisible ceiling. He did not, in his walking, meet any wall.

After ten minutes he stopped.

He stood in the middle of the enormous room. He shone his headlamp in a slow circle. He could see, at the extreme edge of his light's reach, a hint of curvature — some indication that he was in a space that was, indeed, enclosed, if only far enough away that his small light could not, on its own, reach the walls. He estimated, without confidence, that the chamber was perhaps two hundred meters across.

He looked down.

His altimeter read one thousand four hundred and seventy-two meters.

He was, at that moment, deeper than any human being had ever been in this section of the world.

He sat down on a small block.

He turned off his headlamp.

He sat, in the total darkness, and he listened to the breathing.

—

He thought, sitting in the darkness, about his life.

He thought about the small apartment in Bratislava where he lived. He thought about the small orange dog he had had, ten years ago, who had died at fourteen and whom he had never replaced. He thought about the woman he had almost married, at twenty-nine, who had left him because she had understood, before he had, that he was going to spend the rest of his life going into holes in the ground. He thought about the woman he had, in his forties, spent three years with in a companionable way and had, in the end, agreed to part from because they had both wanted, quietly, different things.

He thought about Frantisek. He thought about the aluminum peg. He thought about how he had, at nineteen, wanted Frantisek to say *no. It goes on.*

He thought about the fact that Frantisek had, in the end, been right. Studna at four hundred and eighteen meters had not gone on. It had only gone on because Ondrej Vejr had, on a solo push, forced it to. And it had, from there, kept going, because at some point it had been going to keep going regardless.

He thought about the fact that the cave he was in now was, in a real sense, not Studna anymore. Studna was the cave that ended at four hundred and eighteen meters. Everything below that had been someone else's cave. The cave he was in now — the cave that opened, above the sump, into a passage no one had ever entered — was, he thought, its own thing. It had a different character. It had, above all, a different depth.

He thought about the breathing.

He thought about the fact that he was, at that moment, listening to a sound that he did not have any explanation for, and that he was, in the whole of his experience and training, not able to say what was making it, and that he was not, in the specific quiet clarity of that moment, particularly afraid.

He thought about Milan.

He thought about Katka. He thought about the small careful expedition report he had, over the last month, been drafting in his head about the survey to Chamber Eighteen. He thought about the fact that the expedition report was, at the moment he was sitting in the dark chamber at fourteen hundred and seventy-two meters, no longer going to be written. Someone else was going to write it. Some other caver, some other expedition, in some future year.

He thought about the fact that he was not going up.

He understood this without deliberation. He had understood it, he thought, since he had walked past Milan in Chamber Nineteen and had watched Milan leave. He was going to keep going. He was going to walk into the enormous chamber, and past the enormous chamber, and into whatever was on the far side, and continue down.

He was not going to reach the bottom.

He understood this too. He understood, listening to the breathing, that the passage did not have a bottom. It went down forever. Or it went down for further than he could ever walk. Or it went down to a place he was not going to want to leave. It did not matter which. In each case, he was not going back up.

—

He turned his headlamp back on.

He stood up.

He looked at the small orange notebook in the waterproof case at his hip — the same style of notebook Frantisek had given him at nineteen, the same waterproof case, the same pencil that would not smudge — and he took it out.

He opened it to a blank page.

He wrote, in the small careful hand he had learned from Frantisek:

*Marek Hájek. 15 April, 14:47. Chamber 29. Depth 1472 m. I am continuing alone. Do not look for me. — M.*

He tore the page carefully out of the notebook.

He set the page on the block where he had been sitting. He weighted it with a small stone. He put the notebook back in the case.

He stood.

He looked, once, in the direction he had come from — back up the passage, back toward the eighteen surveyed chambers, back toward the camp at six hundred and the camp at the surface and the small apartment in Bratislava — and he did not, for a moment, feel any particular pull.

He turned around.

He walked into the chamber.

He walked toward the sound of the breathing.

—

He was never found.

The expedition team — Katka, Pavel, Wojciech, the resupply arriving as scheduled on the fifth day — reached the camp at nine hundred meters on the same afternoon Milan and Ana came up from below. Milan told them what had happened. Katka led the search party back down. They found, in the twenty-ninth chamber, the small piece of paper on the block, and they read what Marek had written, and they stood in the chamber for a long time, in the specific silence of cavers who have understood something.

They obeyed him.

They did not look for him.

They came up. They filed, over the following weeks, the small careful expedition report that Marek had never written. The report ended with the discovery of the twenty-ninth chamber at fourteen hundred and seventy-two meters. The report did not mention what lay beyond it. The report did not, at Katka's insistence, permit any further exploration of the passage. The passage was, on the club's map, sealed.

The club did not, in the years that followed, return to that section of the cave. Newer, younger cavers, in later years, tried. They were, individually and collectively, dissuaded by the more senior members. There was, in the caving community of that country, a specific and unusual reluctance to speak about what had happened at the twenty-ninth chamber, and a corresponding reluctance to permit further exploration below it. This reluctance had, over time, hardened into a small quiet consensus.

The cave was, in the language of the club's later reports, *closed at Chamber Twenty-nine.*

Chamber Twenty-nine, and everything below it, was left alone.

The passage, so far as anyone knows, is still descending.

The breathing, so far as anyone has ever gone to listen, has never stopped.

If any caver, in some future decade, chooses to descend past the aluminum peg at four hundred and eighteen meters, and past Ondrej Vejr's small hole in the ceiling, and past the eighteen chambers of the surveyed extension, and into the twenty-ninth chamber at fourteen hundred and seventy-two meters, and to keep going — they may, if they listen carefully at the far edge of the chamber, hear a slow deep rhythmic sound coming from further in. They may, if they follow it, find out what Marek Hájek found.

They may, if they do, come back.

They may, on the whole, not.

The cave is, in the end, patient about this. It has been there for a very long time. It will, so far as anyone knows, be there for a very long time still. There is no hurry. It will accept those who come. It will let alone those who do not.

It is, in this respect, unlike most things.
